description: Ember Bridge is led by Ryan, a full-stack builder and data analyst (data, web, design). We’re tackling MODIS/VIIRS Hot Spots: NASA’s two fire satellites disagree, faking a jump in wildfires after 2012. We’ll build one consistent 25-year fire record for Canada, as open data and an interactive map. Clear plan from day one, real NASA data at the core. Looking for: remote sensing/GIS, data science/ML, video & storytelling. Must be registered at the same local event.
summary:
Ember Bridge keeps 25 years of satellite fire records comparable after MODIS retires. NASA's FIRMS hotspot archive mixes sensors: MODIS (2000 onward) and the more sensitive VIIRS (2012 onward). Raw counts jump in 2012 simply because a new sensor arrived, and Terra's orbit drift creates fake declines. This makes long-term fire trends misleading just as MODIS is being phased out.

We built an open-source pipeline and web app that converts every MODIS hotspot into a "VIIRS-equivalent" weight with a 95% uncertainty range, producing one harmonized monthly fire-activity calendar from 2000 to today. Users can draw any area to see whether a month is unusual and how a fire ranks against history.

We validated it at full resolution on three very different fire regimes: Canadian boreal forest, the Brazilian Amazon and the southern African savanna. On years the model never saw, error drops from about 84% (raw) to 8-10%. Results: the 2012 Canada jump disappears, Amazon 2024 ties the record years 2007 and 2010, and the savanna's 59% Terra drop is shown to be orbit drift, not fewer fires.

This gives emergency managers and researchers a fire history they can trust, whatever the satellite.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ember Bridge turns NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS (Terra/Aqua, 2000 onward) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, 2012 onward) into one harmonized fire-activity record. Each MODIS hotspot gets a "VIIRS-equivalent" weight with a 95% uncertainty range, so a fire in 2003 and a fire in 2024 are counted on the same scale.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Ingest: downloads the full FIRMS archive for each region through the FIRMS API, at full resolution and for every year, with a quota guard.

2. Harmonize: on years when MODIS and VIIRS both flew, the model learns how many VIIRS detections each MODIS detection stands for, by region, season and satellite, including the effect of Terra's orbit drift. Bootstrap resampling gives the 95% range.

3. Build: exports a monthly calendar, fire events and per-area statistics as static files.

4. Web app: a calendar of fire activity from 2000 to today, with a Raw / Harmonized switch. Users can draw any area to see whether a month is unusual and how a fire ranks against history. Hatched cells flag fragile numbers.

VALIDATION

We trained on two regions and tested on the third, and also held out early and late years. On years the model never saw, error is 7.9-10.1%, against 83-84% for raw counts.

RESULTS

- Canada: the false jump in 2012 disappears.

- Brazilian Amazon: 2024 ties the worst years, 2007 and 2010. Raw counts would wrongly call it an all-time record.

- Southern African savanna: Terra's 59% hotspot drop is orbit drift, not fewer fires.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Data from the S-NPP satellite stopped flowing into FIRMS on 2 November 2026, and MODIS ends in 2027. Without a bridge, 25 years of fire history become inconsistent. Ember Bridge gives emergency managers, fire agencies and researchers a trustworthy baseline for questions like "is this season abnormal?" and an honest uncertainty range on every number.

EXAMPLE USE

A fire manager in Canada draws their district on the map and sees that August 2023 was the most active month since 2000, with a 95% range, and how today's largest fire ranks against every past fire. The answer stays valid after MODIS ends, because every year is on the same VIIRS scale.

CREATIVITY

Instead of discarding MODIS or simply rescaling totals, we harmonize each hotspot and show where the result is uncertain. We also validated on three very different fire regimes (boreal forest, tropical deforestation fires, savanna grass fires) to show the method works worldwide.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy), NASA FIRMS API, JavaScript with Leaflet and Leaflet.draw, NASA GIBS satellite imagery as the base map, Netlify hosting, GitHub. The code is open source under the MIT licence.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Sensor sensitivity differences, orbit drift and overpass time, gaps when only one satellite flew (2000-2002), small-number noise, API quotas, and making uncertainty readable for people who are not specialists.

Live app: https://ember-bridge.netlify.app

Code: https://github.com/leo-ntlr/ember-bridge
